claims.text: As-cast eutectic high-entropy alloys predominantly exhibit straight lamellar or rod-like microstructures.
Tailored thermo-mechanical processing can transform a cast lamellar eutectic high-entropy alloy into an ultrafine duplex microstructure.
Combining cold rolling, annealing, and additive manufacturing can produce a kinked, vermicular microstructure from an as-cast lamellar structure.
The proposed processing route will increase hetero-phase boundary density and refine grains.
Tight control of temperature, deformation, cooling rate, and additive-manufacturing energy density is necessary to obtain the desired microstructure and properties.
The intervention is effective only when alloy composition lies within the eutectic range.
Excess oxygen can prevent formation of the targeted vermicular microstructure.
Off-target chemistry can prevent formation of the targeted microstructure.
Insufficient strain or unsuitable annealing conditions will prevent formation of the targeted vermicular microstructure.
The increased phase-boundary density in the vermicular microstructure pins dislocations.
The multi-oriented phase boundaries in the vermicular microstructure arrest microcrack propagation.
Boundary-mediated dislocation accumulation produces strain hardening.
The proposed combined processing route will increase strength beyond current state-of-the-art levels.
The proposed combined processing route will increase ductility beyond current state-of-the-art levels.
The proposed combined processing route will increase Young's modulus beyond current state-of-the-art levels.
The proposed combined processing route will increase fracture resistance beyond current state-of-the-art levels.
The proposed route may produce a greater than 10–20% increase in yield strength relative to conventional processing.
The proposed route may produce a greater than 10–20% increase in Young's modulus relative to conventional processing.
Excessive grain growth or undesirable phase formation will prevent the anticipated mechanical improvements.
Failure to form the intended microstructure, or failure to obtain a statistically significant improvement of at least about 10% in every key property, is designated as falsifying the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The prediction quantifies a greater than 10–20% increase only for yield strength and Young's modulus, while ductility and fracture resistance are merely described as enhanced. The falsification rule nevertheless appears to impose an approximately 10% improvement requirement on all four properties.

The material is framed as an already as-cast lamellar sample that is subsequently processed, but LPBF is a fabrication/remelting route rather than an ordinary post-treatment of such a sample. The sequence by which identical as-cast starting materials undergo a combined cold-rolling, annealing, and LPBF route is therefore internally ambiguous.
